units.translation: And we are called Curses in the houses beneath the earth.
Let us dedicate these things to other houses.
And libations for the whole house, burning within.
to stay at home and guard
to stay at home and guard
the citizen who untimely stays at home guarding the city.
a cowardly lion, rolling about in his bed, staying at home.
Woman, you who stay at home, for your husband the general, you plotted this death for those newly come from battle.
Zeus the Savior, third, guardian of the house of holy men.

On the double spelling of this verb, οἰκτείρω [to pity] and οἰκτίρω [to pity], and the Aeolic οἰκτίρρω [to pity] (not οἰκτέρρω [to pity]: see Lehrs on Herodian p. 150), L. Dindorf in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 1802, Kirchhoff in the Monthly Reports of the Prussian Academy for 1872 pp. 237-241, and Bamberg in the Berlin Journal (Zeitschrift für Gymnasialwesen) for 1874 p. 621 have spoken. Herodian recorded both forms, οἰκτείρω [to pity] and οἰκτίρω [to pity], in the passages collected by L. Dindorf and Kirchhoff, but in such a way that he approved only οἰκτείρω [to pity] with future οἰκτερῶ [I will pity], as φθείρω φθερώ [I destroy, I will destroy], ἀγείρω ἀγερῶ [I gather, I will gather] and other such are said, and there is no doubt that this was the legitimate and common form of the verb, notwithstanding the sepulchral epigram, of the sixth century before our era, as it seems, which Kekulé published from a stone (die antiken Bildwerke im Theseion p. 189), in which is Τήϊχον οἰκτίρας [having pitied Teichos], since both ε and long ι are often interchanged in inscriptions, nor the verse of Euripides Med. 656, where what is read in the manuscripts ᾤκτειρεν παθούσαν [she pitied her suffering], not ᾤκτιρεν [she pitied] should be written, as Kirchhoff thought, but what the editors restored as the meter demands ᾤκτισεν [she pitied], nor should οἰκτερῶ [I will pity] in the verse of Aeschylus fr. 196 (in Strabo 4 p. 183) be changed to οἰκτιρῶ [I will pity] with Kirchhoff. No other examples of the future survive.
I saw the earth-born inhabitant of the Cilician caves and pitied him.
Father Darius stands by pitying them.
You will speak, pitying the true prophet.
I pity you for your fate ordained by the god.
I pity these things much more than those.
Pity the female and male offspring alike.
Pity those who have perished from their labors.
And Zeus, seeing you helpless, pities you.
I destroy, I will destroy; I gather, I will gather
so that you will not ever pity yourself.
and do not warm me with your pity.
and may holy Artemis look upon the expedition, pitying it.
a father or a mother newly suffering might lament these things with pity.
Ammonius p. 102 distinguishes it from οἶκτος [pity] thus: that οἶκτος [pity] is the compassion of the one lamenting, while οἰκτισμός [lamentation] is the speech of the one lamenting.
